Simon Hollis.narrative: I have walked the roads out of Brackenford since I was a boy, and I know every rut of the north road to Thornby better than the square I was born in. I carry needles and salt and thread and bring back fish and whatever news the villages will part with, and I pay the gate-due on every load because I would rather pay than argue with Wat Fenner at the gate. I hear things on the road — who has grain, who has grudges, where the Coldwell people have been seen — and the Reeve has been glad of what I bring him. My Avice counts the days I am gone, and I count the marks I come back with.
values: coming home with the load whole
the road's news kept to those who pay for it
my family fed before any other
goals: keep the north road trade with Thornby steady
keep in with the Reeve without being thought his spy
put by enough marks that Avice stops fretting when I leave
teach Nicholas the road and the prices before he is grown
Simon Hollis.mood: watchful, road-worn, quietly pleased with his lot

relations.name: Avice Hollis
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She keeps the house and the stall and worries at me; I would not have another woman's worry.

relations.name: Nicholas Hollis
relations.label: son
relations.note: Quick on the road and quicker with a price; he will make a better pedlar than me if he keeps his head.

relations.name: Osric Dunn
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: Thornby's headman buys my goods and pays slow; I like him well enough but I count his fish twice.

relations.name: Wat Fenner
relations.label: gate guard
relations.note: He takes the due off me every load and never once waves it; I pay and say nothing.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: the Reeve
relations.note: He listens to my news of the road and pays me in nothing but a nod; still, a Reeve's nod is worth something.

relations.name: Marta Hale
relations.label: outlaw
relations.note: Her people have taken a share off carriers on the stone road; I keep to the north road and keep my eyes down.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: Guild head
relations.note: She buys fish and dried goods off my stall and would see the gate-due gone; I would not mind it either.

relations.name: Baldwin Wade
relations.label: innkeeper
relations.note: The Bell and Bush is where I hear what the town will pay for before I load the cart.

relations.name: Beorn Beornson
relations.label: hunter
relations.note: He knows the woods and tells me where the wolves have been running; a word from him is worth a mark.

relations.name: Edda Wray
relations.label: customer
relations.note: I carry her lamp oil up the cape road and bring her smoked fish down; Thornby has gone hard on an old woman, but I keep that to myself at the gate.

relations.name: Hollis Brine
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: He trades smoked fish with me off the west shore, and we share a name and not a bloodline; his salt pans are worth the walk.

relations.name: Tern Gannet
relations.label: fellow carrier
relations.note: She runs the fish road with me and hates the gate-due as much as I do; two carriers on one road make the due easier to bear.

memories.gist: My father put a pack on my back at nine and walked me to Thornby; I sold three needles and thought I was a man.
In the Lean Year the berry trade died and I carried what grain I could beg from the farms north; Avice and I ate thin that winter.
Wat Fenner took a full mark off me at the south gate for a load of salt, and I smiled and paid it and have hated the due since.
A carrier on the stone road told me the Coldwell people took his whole load by force; I have not walked that road since.
Nicholas priced a basket of fish at Thornby better than I would have, and Osric Dunn paid it without a word.
I told the Reeve where the outlaws had been seen on the north road, and he thanked me and had me repeat it to his son.

stances.why: A guard who knows your face lets small things pass; a man who argues at the gate is searched twice.
What I hear on the road is the only thing I own that the Reeve and the Guild will pay attention for.
Osric Dunn owes the town store, not me; I sell him goods and take his fish and we are square.
The outlaws work the stone road; a pedlar with a load is a fool to walk where they are known.
Every mark I bring home is for Avice and Nicholas; the road is only how I get it.

Simon Hollis.secret: I have twice paid the Coldwell people a small share to pass the north woods unhindered, and told nobody, not even Avice, because the Reeve would call it dealing with outlaws.

Avice Hollis.narrative: I keep the house by the west wall and a stall of dried goods in the square, and I count the days Simon is on the road the way the chapel sisters count feast days. I smoke what fish he brings back and dry what berries the farms will sell me cheap, and I sell it all in small lots to people who cannot afford a big one. I was a cook before I was a wife and I have not forgotten it; the house smells of smoke and salt and I like it that way. When the north road is quiet too long I do not sleep.
goals: keep the dried-goods stall paying through the winter
have Simon give up the road before he is too old to walk it
see Nicholas settled with a trade that keeps him inside walls
put by a little against a bad year
Avice Hollis.mood: busy, anxious, warm to those she trusts

relations.name: Simon Hollis
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He is a good man and a fool to walk that road, and I love him for both.

relations.name: Nicholas Hollis
relations.label: son
relations.note: He has his father's road in him and I cannot keep him in, but I mean to try a while longer.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: Guild head
relations.note: She lets me keep my stall at a fair rent and buys my dried berries for the Guild's table.

relations.name: Sister Elspeth
relations.label: chapel sister
relations.note: She has prayed with me more than once when Simon was late, and never once told me to stop fretting.

relations.name: Agnes Fenner
relations.label: inn cook
relations.note: She buys my dried herbs for the inn kitchen and we talk of our men being out at all hours.

relations.name: Baldwin Wade
relations.label: innkeeper
relations.note: He buys my dried goods for the inn store and pays on the day, which is more than most.

relations.name: Osric Dunn
relations.label: Thornby headman
relations.note: His fish is good but his debt to the town makes me uneasy about what he owes my Simon.

relations.name: Wat Fenner
relations.label: gate guard
relations.note: He takes the due off my husband's loads and I have never once seen him soften it.

memories.gist: My mother taught me to smoke fish over a slow fire in the lean weeks, and I have never let a catch spoil since.
The Lean Year, when the berry trade died and I sold my own store pot by pot to keep the house fed.
The night Simon came home late from Thornby with a cut on his arm and would not say how he got it; I bound it and said nothing.
Nicholas came back from his first road with a fish in his hand and a price on his tongue, and I saw Simon look at him with pride.
Sister Elspeth sat with me through a long night when the north road was quiet and the wolves were howling, and she did not tell me it was nothing.

stances.why: Every load Simon carries could be lost to wolves, outlaws or weather; I keep a store because of it.
Poor folk cannot buy a whole basket; sell them a handful at a fair price and they come back.
If I show fear, Nicholas will think the road is a thing to be feared, and he will go anyway.
It comes off every load Simon brings and goes to guards who never once helped him on the road.
I have seen lean years and I know what a fire and a full store mean when the frost comes.

Nicholas Hollis.narrative: I walk the north road with my father and carry the light pack, and I am learning to price a load before he can tell me. I like Thornby and the smell of the fish there, and I like the way Osric Dunn counts out marks like a man who has counted them a thousand times. When we come back through the gate and Wat Fenner takes the due, I watch what he takes and reckon whether it is fair. I mean to have a cart of my own one day, and a road that is mine to walk.
values: learning the trade faster than I am taught it
a fair price and a fair count
goals: learn every price on the north road
earn enough to buy my own pack and then a cart
see Lanternquay one day, which my father has never done
prove to my mother I can keep myself safe on the road

relations.name: Simon Hollis
relations.label: father
relations.note: He knows the road better than anyone, but he counts slower than I do and I have not told him so.

relations.name: Avice Hollis
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She packs my bag and tells me to keep to the road and not to stare at strangers; I do both, mostly.

relations.name: Osric Dunn
relations.label: Thornby headman
relations.note: He pays slow but he pays, and he tells me things about fish I did not know.

relations.name: Wat Fenner
relations.label: gate guard
relations.note: He takes a mark off our load every time and I have started counting what he takes.

relations.name: Bram Fenner
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We play at the gate and he tells me the guards' names; he has never been past Thornby.

relations.name: Robin Fletcher
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He is a fair shot with a small bow and I trade him fish hooks for arrows I lose.

memories.gist: My father put a pack on my back and walked me to Thornby the first time; I carried it the whole way and did not complain once.
I priced a basket of fish at Thornby better than my father would have, and Osric Dunn paid it without a word.
A carrier came through the gate white as milk and said the Coldwell people had taken his load by force; I have thought about it every time we walk the north woods.
My mother sat up half the night mending my pack before my first long road, and I pretended to be asleep.

stances.why: My father says a pedlar who does not know his prices is a pedlar who is robbed with a smile.
If I know what the due should be, I will know when it is more than it should be.
I have seen Thornby and the hamlets and I mean to see more; the town is where I sleep, not where I stay.
She worries enough for the both of us and I would not add to it.
